region_scene_page.compact: A stripped 1950s guitar-and-slapback lane where country boogie, blues, R&B, and hillbilly flash become urgent rock records.
region_scene_page.standard: Rockabilly came out of small labels, Southern studios, young players, and quick takes that prized feel over polish. Sun Records is the best-known center, but the vocabulary spreads through Carl Perkins, Gene Vincent, Johnny Burnette, Eddie Cochran, Duane Eddy, Link Wray, and other records that make guitar attitude the event. Compared with broader early rock, this lane feels more wiry and local: slapped bass, echo, hiccuped vocals, lean drums, sharp guitar breaks, and very little orchestral cushion.

region_scene_page.standard: The Brill Building label points to a New York songwriting-and-publishing system more than to one literal room or one fixed sound. Around the late 1950s and early 1960s, writers and teams around the Broadway/Times Square publishing world—Goffin/King, Greenwich/Barry, Mann/Weil, Bacharach/David, and others—worked with producers, A&R people, labels, and performers to create records for girl groups, teen idols, pop-soul singers, and dance-craze acts. The girl-group side sharpened the formula: big hooks, direct teenage feeling, cinematic mini-dramas, handclaps, call-and-response, dramatic intros, and production that could make a small song feel huge. Professional song factories: writers, producers, publishers, and performers often had separate roles. Teen emotion made cinematic: love, jealousy, social pressure, devotion, heartbreak, and rebellion compressed into quick scenes. Girl-group perspective: many songs foregrounded young female voice, desire, uncertainty, and defiance even when written by adult teams. Compact architecture: short intros, immediate hooks, bridges that escalate the stakes, and final choruses that resolve or intensify the drama. Studio drama: percussion, handclaps, strings, echo, stacked backing vocals, and Spector-style density could turn a radio single into a world. Bridge behavior: the archetype touches doo-wop, early soul-pop, Motown, teen-idol radio, singer-songwriter craft, power pop, and modern pop factories.

region_scene_page.compact: A 1960s ornate-pop road where chamber instruments, studio craft, close harmony, and emotional precision make pop feel miniature and grand at once.
region_scene_page.standard: Baroque pop does not mean classical music pasted onto rock. The Beach Boys, Left Banke, Zombies, Love, Procol Harum, and early Bee Gees each approach that glow differently. The lane is polished but fragile: orchestration, harmony, and bittersweet melody matter more than volume or jam energy.

region_scene_page.compact: A late-1960s pop-rock road where hooks, harmonies, studio effects, and counterculture color make familiar song forms feel unreal.
region_scene_page.standard: Psychedelic pop is not only long jams and acid-rock heaviness. region_scene_page.compact: A downtown New York scene/ecosystem where punk urgency, art-school experiment, poetry, pop instincts, minimal electronics, and club culture collided around CBGB and nearby venues rather than resolving into one sound.
region_scene_page.standard: CBGB opened in 1973 on the Bowery under Hilly Kristal and became a practical home for original underground rock. What later looks like “the CBGB sound” was actually a cluster of incompatible but mutually intensifying bands: Patti Smith fused rock and poetry; Television stretched guitar interplay into nervous art-rock; Talking Heads turned anxiety, rhythm, and conceptual framing into new wave; Blondie smuggled girl-group/pop/disco instincts through downtown cool; Richard Hell gave punk a persona of damaged refusal; Suicide reduced rock to voice, synth pulse, and menace; and No Wave pushed the scene toward abrasive boundary testing. Scene before sound: bands shared rooms, audience, press, and permission structure more than a single musical grammar. Original-song rule: the venue became a testing ground for bands that did not fit cover-band or arena-rock economics. Art-punk plurality: poetry-rock, nervous funk, pop-art new wave, guitar abstraction, minimal synth menace, and No Wave abrasion all sit in the same historical neighborhood. Anti-classic-rock scale: short sets, small rooms, stripped gear, weird personas, and direct performance replaced virtuoso sprawl. Bridge behavior: the archetype points backward to first-wave punk/proto-punk and forward to post-punk, new wave, college rock, noise-rock, synth-punk, and indie art-rock. Fit caution: an Atlas user may love Blondie or Talking Heads while rejecting Suicide/No Wave, or love Television while rejecting broader punk.
